title: Femoral Triangle
definition: A triangular subfascial space situated in the anteromedial aspect of the upper one-third of the thigh.
key_points: Boundaries: Inguinal ligament (superior), Sartorius muscle (lateral), Adductor longus muscle (medial).
Contents: Femoral nerve, Femoral artery, Femoral vein, and deep inguinal lymph nodes (lateral to medial).
Clinical significance: Site for checking femoral pulse, compressing femoral artery to control bleeding, and femoral hernia.

title: Right Atrium of Heart
definition: One of the four chambers of the human heart, receiving deoxygenated blood from the systemic circulation.
key_points: Receives blood from: Superior Vena Cava (SVC), Inferior Vena Cava (IVC), and Coronary Sinus.
Internal features: Sinus venarum (smooth posterior part), Pectinate muscles (rough anterior part), and Fossa ovalis on the interatrial septum.
SA Node: Located in the upper part of the sulcus terminalis near the opening of the SVC.

title: Deltoid Muscle
definition: A large, triangular muscle covering the shoulder joint, giving the shoulder its rounded contour.
key_points: Origin: Clavicle (anterior part), Acromion (middle part), and Spine of Scapula (posterior part).
Insertion: Deltoid tuberosity on the lateral aspect of the shaft of the humerus.
Action: Major abductor of the arm (middle fibers, from 15 to 90 degrees), flexion (anterior fibers), extension (posterior fibers).
Nerve supply: Axillary nerve (C5, C6).

title: Hepatic Portal Vein
definition: A short, wide blood vessel that carries nutrient-rich blood from the gastrointestinal tract and spleen to the liver.
key_points: Formation: Formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of the Superior Mesenteric Vein and the Splenic Vein.
Course: Runs upwards behind the first part of the duodenum in the free margin of the lesser omentum.
Tributaries: Left gastric vein, Right gastric vein, and Cystic vein.
Clinical significance: Portal hypertension causes varices in the esophagus, stomach, and rectum (hemorrhoids).

title: Action Potential
definition: A rapid change in membrane potential that propagates along the surface of a cell (neuron or muscle fiber).
key_points: Resting state: Resting membrane potential is typically -70mV in neurons, maintained by Na+/K+ ATPase pump.
Depolarization: Opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels allows Na+ influx, changing potential toward +30mV.
Repolarization: Closing of Na+ channels and opening of voltage-gated K+ channels allows K+ efflux, returning potential toward resting levels.
Hyperpolarization: Transient state where potential becomes more negative than resting potential due to delayed K+ channel closing.

title: Erythropoiesis
definition: The complex process of origin, development, and maturation of Red Blood Cells (Erythrocytes) in the red bone marrow.
key_points: Site: Yolk sac (mesoblastic stage in embryo), Liver/Spleen (hepatic stage in fetus), and Red Bone Marrow (myeloid stage post-birth).
Stages: Proerythroblast -> Early Normoblast -> Intermediate Normoblast (hemoglobin begins) -> Late Normoblast (nucleus extruded) -> Reticulocyte -> Erythrocyte.
Regulation: Stimulated by Erythropoietin (EPO), a hormone released by renal peritubular cells in response to hypoxia.
Factors: Vitamin B12 and Folic acid are essential for DNA synthesis; Iron is essential for hemoglobin synthesis.

title: Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
definition: The volume of fluid filtered from the glomerular capillaries into Bowman's capsule per unit time.
key_points: Normal value: Approximately 125 mL/min (or 180 Liters/day) in healthy adult males.
Determinants: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (promotes filtration), Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure (opposes), and glomerular capillary colloid osmotic pressure (opposes).
Autoregulation: Maintained constant between renal arterial pressures of 80-180 mmHg via myogenic mechanism and tubuloglomerular feedback.

title: Succussion
definition: The act of shaking liquid homeopathic preparations vigorously with impact, used to potentize soluble substances.
key_points: Process: Involves serial dilution of the substance in alcohol/purified water, followed by 10 strong downward strokes against a resilient leather pad.
Purpose: Homoeopathic philosophy states that succussion releases the latent dynamic healing power of the substance.
Potency scales: Used in Centesimal (C), Decimal (D/X), and 50-Millesimal (LM) potency preparation.

title: Trituration
definition: The process of reducing insoluble solid substances to soluble potencies by grinding them with lactose (sugar of milk) in a mortar and pestle.
key_points: Substances: Minerals (e.g. Silicea, Sulphur) and certain insoluble plant/animal materials.
Standard timing: A standard trituration step takes 1 hour, divided into three stages of 20 minutes each (scraping, mixing, grinding).
Solubility limit: Insoluble substances become soluble in water/alcohol after reaching the 6C or 8X trituration level.

title: Maceration
definition: A cold extraction process used in homeopathy to prepare mother tinctures from fresh, moisture-rich plant or animal substances.
key_points: Duration: Requires placing the finely chopped drug substance in contact with solvent (alcohol/water) for 2 to 4 weeks.
Apparatus: Conducted in wide-mouthed, hermetically closed glass or stoneware jars.
Extraction mechanism: Solvent penetrates the tissues, dissolving soluble active principles; supernatant is then decanted and pressed out.
